questions.sec: Disease Types, Pneumoconiosis Definition, the Dust-Particle Size/Site Table, the Four Pneumoconioses and Byssinosis (Organic Dust, Monday Fever)
questions.q: Which three disease groups are listed under 'Types' at the start of page 223?
opts: Pneumoconiosis, occupational asthma and hypersensitivity pneumonitis
Pneumoconiosis, silicosis and asbestosis
Pneumoconiosis, occupational asthma and byssinosis
Occupational asthma, hypersensitivity pneumonitis and Caplan syndrome
questions.exp: The opening list reads 'Types : Pneumoconiosis. occupational asthma. Hypersensitive pneumonitis.' Silicosis and asbestosis are subtypes of pneumoconiosis listed further down the page, not parallel categories. (Book p223)

questions.sec: Disease Types, Pneumoconiosis Definition, the Dust-Particle Size/Site Table, the Four Pneumoconioses and Byssinosis (Organic Dust, Monday Fever)
questions.q: How is pneumoconiosis defined on page 223?
opts: Accumulation of silica in the pleura with plaque formation
Accumulation of dust in lung and tissue reactions to its presence
Accumulation of dust in lung without any tissue reaction
Accumulation of organic dust in the alveoli with granuloma formation
questions.exp: The definition reads 'accumulation of dust in lung & tissue reactions to its presence'. The tissue reaction is part of the definition, which is why the chapter separates the dusts by the pattern of reaction they provoke. (Book p223)

questions.sec: Disease Types, Pneumoconiosis Definition, the Dust-Particle Size/Site Table, the Four Pneumoconioses and Byssinosis (Organic Dust, Monday Fever)
questions.q: Match each dust-particle size with its printed deposition site — 1) >3 µm 2) 0.5–3 µm 3) <0.5 µm … A) Alveoli B) Bronchiole C) Secondary bronchi
questions.exp: The table reads '>3 µm — Secondary bronchi', '0.5–3 µm — Bronchiole' and '<0.5 µm — Alveoli'. The finest particles penetrate furthest, which is why alveolar dusts cause the pneumoconioses. (Book p223)

questions.sec: Disease Types, Pneumoconiosis Definition, the Dust-Particle Size/Site Table, the Four Pneumoconioses and Byssinosis (Organic Dust, Monday Fever)
questions.q: Which pneumoconiosis is marked as the most common on page 223?
opts: Coal worker pneumoconiosis
Asbestosis
Berylliosis
Silicosis
questions.exp: The list reads '1. Silicosis : most common. 2. Asbestosis. 3. Coal worker pneumoconiosis (CWP). 4. Berylliosis.' The following page devotes a full risk-factor and table section to silicosis accordingly. (Book p223)

questions.sec: Disease Types, Pneumoconiosis Definition, the Dust-Particle Size/Site Table, the Four Pneumoconioses and Byssinosis (Organic Dust, Monday Fever)
questions.q: What does the page 223 note say about byssinosis?
opts: It is hypersensitivity to organic dust exposure, with egg-shell calcification as its clinical feature
It is hypersensitivity to organic dust exposure, with recurrent Monday fever as its clinical feature
It is hypersensitivity to inorganic dust exposure, with recurrent Monday fever as its clinical feature
It is a pneumoconiosis from cotton dust, with progressive massive fibrosis as its clinical feature
questions.exp: The note reads 'Byssinosis : Hypersensitivity to organic dust exposure' and 'Clinical features : Recurrent monday fever.' Monday fever describes the symptoms recurring on the first day back at work after the weekend. (Book p223)

questions.sec: Disease Types, Pneumoconiosis Definition, the Dust-Particle Size/Site Table, the Four Pneumoconioses and Byssinosis (Organic Dust, Monday Fever)
questions.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — three are printed as types of pneumoconiosis on page 223, one is listed separately as organic-dust hypersensitivity:
opts: Berylliosis
Asbestosis
Silicosis
Byssinosis
questions.exp: The numbered pneumoconiosis list is silicosis, asbestosis, coal worker pneumoconiosis and berylliosis. Byssinosis appears only in the Note as hypersensitivity to organic dust — a different mechanism from dust accumulation with fibrosis. (Book p223)

questions.sec: Disease Types, Pneumoconiosis Definition, the Dust-Particle Size/Site Table, the Four Pneumoconioses and Byssinosis (Organic Dust, Monday Fever)
questions.q: Particles larger than 3 µm are deposited in the ______, according to the page 223 table.
opts: Alveoli
Pleura
Secondary bronchi
Bronchioles
questions.exp: The table pairs '>3 µm' with 'Secondary bronchi'. Particles of 0.5–3 µm reach the bronchiole and those below 0.5 µm reach the alveoli, which is where the interstitial reactions begin. (Book p223)

questions.sec: Silicosis: Industries, Crystalline vs Amorphous Silica, Parenchymal-Only Involvement, Malignancy/COPD Risk and the Acute-vs-Chronic Table (Exposure, Pathogenesis, Clinical Triangle, BAL, PFT, Prognosis)
questions.q: Which industries are listed as silicosis risk factors on page 224?
opts: Mining industry, quarries, blast furnaces, slate industry, sand stone industry, ceramics and rock cutting
Mining industry, battery manufacturing and textile industry
Textile industry, cement industry, ship building work and automobile industry
Ceramic industry, battery manufacturing and alloy industry
questions.exp: The risk-factor list reads 'mining industry, Quarries, Blast furnaces, Slate industry, Sand stone industry, Ceramics, Rock cutting'. The textile/cement/shipbuilding list belongs to asbestosis on page 227 and the ceramic/battery/alloy list to berylliosis on page 229. (Book p224)

questions.sec: Silicosis: Industries, Crystalline vs Amorphous Silica, Parenchymal-Only Involvement, Malignancy/COPD Risk and the Acute-vs-Chronic Table (Exposure, Pathogenesis, Clinical Triangle, BAL, PFT, Prognosis)
questions.q: Which type of silica is most common, what is its composition, and which carries the higher occupational hazard?
opts: Crystalline silica (cristobalite); SiO2 (combined silica); higher risk of occupational hazard
Crystalline silica (quartz); SiO2 (free silica); higher risk of occupational hazard
Amorphous silica; SiO2 bound in silicates; higher risk of occupational hazard
Crystalline silica (quartz); SiO2 (free silica); lower risk of occupational hazard
questions.exp: The block reads '1. Crystalline silica (Quartz) : m/c', 'Composition : SiO2 (Free silica)' and 'Higher risk of occupational hazard', with '2. Amorphous silica' as the second, lesser type. (Book p224)

questions.sec: Silicosis: Industries, Crystalline vs Amorphous Silica, Parenchymal-Only Involvement, Malignancy/COPD Risk and the Acute-vs-Chronic Table (Exposure, Pathogenesis, Clinical Triangle, BAL, PFT, Prognosis)
questions.q: Two features are printed for silicosis under 'FEATURES': lung parenchymal involvement with ______ pleural involvement, and a risk of malignancy and COPD.
opts: Bilateral
Extensive
No
Unilateral
questions.exp: The line reads 'Lung parenchymal involvement (No pleural involvement)' and the next 'Risk of malignancy and COPD.' The absence of pleural disease is a printed point of contrast with asbestosis, which is dominated by pleural plaques. (Book p224)

questions.sec: Silicosis: Industries, Crystalline vs Amorphous Silica, Parenchymal-Only Involvement, Malignancy/COPD Risk and the Acute-vs-Chronic Table (Exposure, Pathogenesis, Clinical Triangle, BAL, PFT, Prognosis)
questions.q: The acute-versus-chronic silicosis table gives two exposure durations. Which pair is printed?
opts: Large quantity for 2 years (acute) versus 10–30 years (chronic)
Large quantity for 5 years (acute) versus 20–40 years (chronic)
Large quantity for 2 years (acute) versus 5–10 years (chronic)
Small quantity for 2 years (acute) versus 10–30 years (chronic)
questions.exp: The exposure row reads 'Large quantity for 2 years' for acute silicosis and 'For 10–30 years' for chronic silicosis. The acute form needs an intense exposure over a short period, not a small one. (Book p224)

questions.sec: Silicosis: Industries, Crystalline vs Amorphous Silica, Parenchymal-Only Involvement, Malignancy/COPD Risk and the Acute-vs-Chronic Table (Exposure, Pathogenesis, Clinical Triangle, BAL, PFT, Prognosis)
questions.q: Which pathogenesis chain is printed for chronic silicosis in the table?
opts: Injury to capillary endothelium → alveolar haemorrhage and autoimmune illness (SLE, RA)
Injury to type II pneumocytes → progressive massive fibrosis and bronchogenic carcinoma
Injury to pulmonary alveolar macrophages → silicotuberculosis (primary TB) and immune deficiency (HIV)
Injury to pulmonary alveolar macrophages → silicotuberculosis (reactivation of latent TB) and autoimmune illness (SLE, RA)
questions.exp: The chronic pathogenesis cell reads 'Injury to pulmonary alveolar macrophages', with a double-headed arrow to 'Silicotuberculosis (Reactivation of latent TB)' on one side and 'Autoimmune illness (SLE, RA)' on the other. The acute cell in the same row is printed as a dash. (Book p224)

questions.sec: Silicosis: Industries, Crystalline vs Amorphous Silica, Parenchymal-Only Involvement, Malignancy/COPD Risk and the Acute-vs-Chronic Table (Exposure, Pathogenesis, Clinical Triangle, BAL, PFT, Prognosis)
questions.q: In chronic silicosis, what frequency of chest signs is printed?
opts: 25% of cases
45% of cases
15% of cases
50% of cases
questions.exp: The chronic clinical cell reads 'Chornic dry cough', 'Dyspnea on exertion' and 'Chest signs in 25% cases'. Most patients therefore have no chest signs despite established radiological disease. (Book p224)

questions.sec: Silicosis: Industries, Crystalline vs Amorphous Silica, Parenchymal-Only Involvement, Malignancy/COPD Risk and the Acute-vs-Chronic Table (Exposure, Pathogenesis, Clinical Triangle, BAL, PFT, Prognosis)
questions.q: Match each table row with its acute-silicosis entry — 1) Clinical features 2) Investigations 3) Prognosis … A) PAS positive milky white BAL B) Very poor C) Acute onset with severe dyspnea, hypoxia and weight loss
questions.exp: Acute silicosis gives 'Acute onset : severe dyspnea, hypoxia, weight loss', 'PAS positive milky white BAL (Bronchoalveolar lavage)' and 'very poor' prognosis. The chronic column instead reads PFT with a mixed pattern and a dash for prognosis. (Book p224)

questions.sec: Silicosis: Industries, Crystalline vs Amorphous Silica, Parenchymal-Only Involvement, Malignancy/COPD Risk and the Acute-vs-Chronic Table (Exposure, Pathogenesis, Clinical Triangle, BAL, PFT, Prognosis)
questions.q: A sandblaster develops breathlessness, hypoxia and weight loss within two years, and lavage returns milky white PAS-positive fluid. Which diagnosis and prognostic statement match the page 224 table?
opts: Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, with a very poor prognosis
Acute silicosis, with a very poor prognosis
Byssinosis, with recurrent Monday fever
Chronic silicosis, with a mixed pattern on spirometry
questions.exp: The acute column combines 'Large quantity for 2 years', the dyspnea-hypoxia-weight loss triangle, 'PAS positive milky white BAL' and 'very poor' prognosis. Milky white PAS-positive lavage also appears under PAP on page 226, but the two-year heavy exposure and clinical triangle here are the printed acute-silicosis set. (Book p224)

questions.sec: Radiology of Silicosis: Acute Crazy-Pavement CT Pattern and the Chronic Nodule-to-PMF Sequence with Egg-Shell Calcification and Upper Lobe ILD
questions.q: Which three components make up the 'crazy pavement appearance' printed for acute silicosis on CT?
opts: Ground glass opacifications with destroyed lung structure, thin septa and multiple large nodules in pleura
Ground glass opacifications with intact structure of lung, thickened septa and multiple subpleural bullae
Consolidation with air bronchograms, thickened pleura and multiple centrilobular nodules
Ground glass opacifications with intact structure of lung, thickened septa and multiple centrilobular small nodules in parenchyma
questions.exp: The CT panel is labelled 'Crazy pavement appearance : Ground glass opacifications (Intact structure of lung); Thickened septa; multiple centrilobular small nodules in parenchyma.' The preserved lung architecture distinguishes it from destructive fibrosis. (Book p225)

questions.sec: Radiology of Silicosis: Acute Crazy-Pavement CT Pattern and the Chronic Nodule-to-PMF Sequence with Egg-Shell Calcification and Upper Lobe ILD
questions.q: Which radiological progression is printed for chronic silicosis on page 225?
opts: Small unilateral asymmetric nodules → large conglomerate nodules (holly leaf appearance) + hilar lymphadenopathy with popcorn calcification → PMF, plus upper lobe interstitial lung disease
Large bilateral asymmetric nodules → small centrilobular nodules with angel wing appearance + hilar lymphadenopathy with egg shell calcification → PMF, plus lower lobe interstitial lung disease

Small bilateral symmetric centrilobular parenchymal nodules → large conglomerate nodules (angel wing appearance) ± cavitations + hilar lymphadenopathy with egg shell calcification → progressive massive fibrosis (PMF), plus upper lobe interstitial lung disease

Small bilateral symmetric centrilobular nodules → large conglomerate nodules (angel wing appearance) ± cavitations + hilar lymphadenopathy with egg shell calcification → PMF, plus lower lobe interstitial lung disease
questions.exp: The film sequence on page 225 reads exactly from 'Small bilateral symmetric centrilobular parenchymal nodule' to 'Large conglomerate nodules (Angel wing appearance)' to '± Cavitations + Hilar lymphadenopathy with egg shell calcification' to 'Progressive massive fibrosis (PMF)', ending with 'upper lobe interstitial lung disease'. (Book p225)

questions.sec: Radiology of Silicosis: Acute Crazy-Pavement CT Pattern and the Chronic Nodule-to-PMF Sequence with Egg-Shell Calcification and Upper Lobe ILD
questions.q: The hilar node calcification of chronic silicosis on page 225 is described as ______ calcification.
opts: Egg shell
Holly leaf
Candle dripping
Popcorn
questions.exp: The label reads 'Hilar lymphadenopathy with egg shell calcification'. The hilar nodes calcify peripherally, giving a thin shell rather than a solid or popcorn density. (Book p225)

questions.sec: Radiology of Silicosis: Acute Crazy-Pavement CT Pattern and the Chronic Nodule-to-PMF Sequence with Egg-Shell Calcification and Upper Lobe ILD
questions.q: The large conglomerate nodules of chronic silicosis are described by which appearance on page 225?
opts: Crazy pavement appearance
Angel wing appearance
Shaggy heart appearance
Holly leaf appearance
questions.exp: The caption reads 'Large conglomerate nodules (Angel wing appearance)'. Holly leaf and shaggy heart are the asbestos signs printed on page 227, and crazy pavement is the acute silicosis CT pattern. (Book p225)

questions.sec: Radiology of Silicosis: Acute Crazy-Pavement CT Pattern and the Chronic Nodule-to-PMF Sequence with Egg-Shell Calcification and Upper Lobe ILD
questions.q: TRUE or FALSE about the two silicosis patterns on page 225.
opts: True — the chronic pattern is confined to the lower lobes
False — both patterns are described as crazy pavement on CT
False — the acute pattern is nodular progression to PMF, whereas the chronic pattern is crazy pavement
True — the acute pattern is a CT crazy-pavement appearance, whereas the chronic pattern progresses through nodules to PMF
questions.exp: The acute column holds the single CT image captioned 'Crazy pavement appearance', while the chronic column holds the full film sequence of nodules → conglomerate nodules → PMF. The same chronic column ends with 'upper lobe interstitial lung disease'. (Book p225)

questions.sec: Radiology of Silicosis: Acute Crazy-Pavement CT Pattern and the Chronic Nodule-to-PMF Sequence with Egg-Shell Calcification and Upper Lobe ILD
questions.q: A quarry worker with 20 years of exposure has a chest film showing small symmetric nodules and egg-shell hilar calcification, and a CT showing upper lobe fibrosis. Which staging does page 225 support?
opts: Chronic silicosis with progressive massive fibrosis and upper lobe interstitial lung disease
Acute silicosis with crazy pavement pattern and milky white lavage
Chronic asbestosis with pleural plaques and lower lobe fibrosis
Coal worker pneumoconiosis with Caplan syndrome
questions.exp: The chronic column of page 225 runs from the symmetric centrilobular nodules to conglomerate nodules with egg-shell hilar calcification to PMF, ending with upper lobe interstitial lung disease. Pleural plaques, by contrast, are the asbestos hallmark on page 227. (Book p225)

questions.sec: Crazy-Pavement Differential (DAH, AEP, PAP with Anti-GM-CSF), Coal Workers Pneumoconiosis, the CWP-vs-Silicosis Table and Caplan Syndrome
questions.q: Which conditions are listed on page 226 as showing a crazy pavement pattern of lung?
opts: Diffuse alveolar damage (DAD), allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis and pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP)
Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (DAH), acute eosinophilic pneumonia (AEP) and pulmonary alveolar microlithiasis
Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (DAH), hypersensitivity pneumonitis and sarcoidosis
Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (DAH), acute eosinophilic pneumonia (AEP) and pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP)
questions.exp: The note lists 'Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (DAH)', 'Acute eosinophilic pneumonia (AEP)' and 'Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP)'. DAD and ABPA are not printed in this differential. (Book p226)

questions.sec: Crazy-Pavement Differential (DAH, AEP, PAP with Anti-GM-CSF), Coal Workers Pneumoconiosis, the CWP-vs-Silicosis Table and Caplan Syndrome
questions.q: What mechanism and lavage finding are printed for pulmonary alveolar proteinosis on page 226?
opts: Deficiency of GM-CSF receptors causing abnormal clearance of surfactant, with PAS positive milky white BAL
Antibodies against GM-CSF causing abnormal clearance of surfactant, with PAS positive milky white BAL
Antibodies against GM-CSF causing excessive surfactant production, with PAS negative thin BAL
Antibodies against surfactant protein-A causing abnormal clearance of surfactant, with PAS positive milky white BAL
questions.exp: The PAP entry reads 'Antibodies against GM-CSF (Abnormal clearance of surfactant)' and 'PAS positive milky white BAL'. The defect is impaired macrophage clearance of surfactant driven by neutralising anti-GM-CSF antibodies. (Book p226)

questions.sec: Crazy-Pavement Differential (DAH, AEP, PAP with Anti-GM-CSF), Coal Workers Pneumoconiosis, the CWP-vs-Silicosis Table and Caplan Syndrome
questions.q: Which four features are printed as similarities between CWP and silicosis?
opts: Upper lobe involvement, injury to type II pneumocytes causing TB or autoimmune disease, ↑COPD, and pleural plaques ± calcification progressing to PMF
Upper lobe involvement, injury to PAMs causing TB or autoimmune disease, ↑COPD, and parenchymal nodules (<0.5 cm) with no cavitation
Upper lobe involvement, injury to PAMs causing TB or autoimmune disease, ↑COPD, and parenchymal nodules (>1 cm) ± cavitations progressing to PMF
Lower lobe involvement, injury to PAMs causing TB or autoimmune disease, ↓COPD, and parenchymal nodules (>3 cm) ± cavitations progressing to PMF
questions.exp: The block reads 'Upper lobe involvement', 'Injury to PAMs → TB or autoimmune disease', '↑ COPD' and 'Parenchymal nodules (>1 cm) ± cavitations → PMF'. CWP is AKA black lung from coal dust exposure, with black pigmentation and fibrosis due to carbon pigment. (Book p226)

questions.sec: Crazy-Pavement Differential (DAH, AEP, PAP with Anti-GM-CSF), Coal Workers Pneumoconiosis, the CWP-vs-Silicosis Table and Caplan Syndrome
questions.q: The CWP-versus-silicosis table on page 226 has exactly three rows. Which set of entries is printed?
opts: Malignancy association present in silicosis and absent in CWP; hilar lymphadenopathy absent in silicosis and present in CWP; Caplan syndrome absent in silicosis and present in CWP
Malignancy association absent in silicosis and present in CWP; hilar lymphadenopathy present in silicosis and absent in CWP; Caplan syndrome present in silicosis and absent in CWP
Malignancy association present in silicosis and absent in CWP; hilar lymphadenopathy present in both; Caplan syndrome present in both
Malignancy association present in both; hilar lymphadenopathy absent in silicosis and present in CWP; Caplan syndrome absent in silicosis and present in CWP
questions.exp: The table reads: 'Association with malignancy — Present (silicosis), Absent (CWP)'; 'Hilar lymphadenopathy — Absent (silicosis), Present (CWP)'; 'Caplan syndrome — Absent (silicosis), Present (CWP)'. This hilar row contradicts the chronic silicosis film label on page 225, a source inconsistency recorded in the caveat file. (Book p226)

questions.sec: Crazy-Pavement Differential (DAH, AEP, PAP with Anti-GM-CSF), Coal Workers Pneumoconiosis, the CWP-vs-Silicosis Table and Caplan Syndrome
questions.q: Which three components make up Caplan syndrome on page 226?
opts: Silicosis (necrobiotic nodule) + rheumatoid arthritis with IgM rheumatoid factor positive + active synovitis
Coal worker pneumoconiosis (necrobiotic nodule) + rheumatoid arthritis with IgA rheumatoid factor positive + inactive synovitis
Coal worker pneumoconiosis (necrobiotic nodule) + systemic lupus erythematosus with IgA rheumatoid factor positive + active synovitis
Coal worker pneumoconiosis (necrobiotic nodule) + rheumatoid arthritis with IgA rheumatoid factor positive + active synovitis
questions.exp: The syndrome is spelled out as 'Coal worker pneumoconiosis (Necrobiotic nodule)' plus 'Rheumatoid arthritis : IgA rheumatoid factor positive' plus 'Active synovitis'. The serotype is IgA, and the arthritis must be active. (Book p226)

questions.sec: Crazy-Pavement Differential (DAH, AEP, PAP with Anti-GM-CSF), Coal Workers Pneumoconiosis, the CWP-vs-Silicosis Table and Caplan Syndrome
questions.q: A coal miner with rheumatoid arthritis has multiple peripheral lung nodules with cavitation. Which eponym applies, and what is the printed nodule size threshold for CWP?
opts: Silicosis with rheumatoid arthritis; CWP nodules are >1 cm
Caplan syndrome; CWP nodules are >3 cm
Caplan syndrome; CWP nodules are >1 cm
Caplan syndrome; CWP nodules are >1 mm
questions.exp: Caplan syndrome is defined on page 226 as CWP with a necrobiotic nodule, rheumatoid arthritis (IgA rheumatoid factor positive) and active synovitis. The same page prints parenchymal nodules '(>1 cm) ± cavitations → PMF' for CWP. (Book p226)

questions.sec: Crazy-Pavement Differential (DAH, AEP, PAP with Anti-GM-CSF), Coal Workers Pneumoconiosis, the CWP-vs-Silicosis Table and Caplan Syndrome
questions.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — three of these are printed under the page 226 crazy-pavement differential, one is not:
opts: Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage
Hypersensitivity pneumonitis
Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis
Acute eosinophilic pneumonia
questions.exp: The differential lists DAH, AEP and PAP only. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis appears on page 228 as a cause of non-caseating granuloma, a different list. (Book p226)

questions.sec: Chronic Asbestosis: Fibre Types, Industries, Pleural Plaques (Candle Dripping, Holly Leaf), BAPE Fluid Criteria, Crow Feet Sign, Shaggy Heart Sign and Parenchymal Fibrosis
questions.q: Match each fibre with its printed description on page 227 — 1) Serpentile/chrysotile 2) Crocidolite 3) Amosite … A) 90% of fibres, curly strands, less toxic B) Amphibole named first on the 10% limb C) Amphibole marked more dangerous
questions.exp: The diagram reads 'Asbestos fibres' with a 90% limb to 'Serpentile/chrysotile (Curly strands) — Less toxic' and a 10% limb to 'Amphibole (Brittle long straight rods)', splitting into 'Crocidolite' and 'Amosite (more dangerous)'. Chrysotile is the only serpentine form listed. (Book p227)

questions.sec: Chronic Asbestosis: Fibre Types, Industries, Pleural Plaques (Candle Dripping, Holly Leaf), BAPE Fluid Criteria, Crow Feet Sign, Shaggy Heart Sign and Parenchymal Fibrosis
questions.q: Which amphibole is marked as more dangerous on page 227, and which two amphiboles are named?
opts: Crocidolite is marked more dangerous; the two amphiboles are crocidolite and amosite
Amosite is marked more dangerous; the two amphiboles are crocidolite and amosite
Amosite is marked more dangerous; the two amphiboles are amosite and tremolite
Chrysotile is marked more dangerous; the two amphiboles are chrysotile and amosite
questions.exp: The amphibole limb names 'Crocidolite' and 'Amosite (more dangerous)'. Chrysotile sits on the serpentine limb and is labelled less toxic. (Book p227)

questions.sec: Chronic Asbestosis: Fibre Types, Industries, Pleural Plaques (Candle Dripping, Holly Leaf), BAPE Fluid Criteria, Crow Feet Sign, Shaggy Heart Sign and Parenchymal Fibrosis
questions.q: Match each pleural finding with its printed description — 1) Pleural plaques 2) Visceral pleural calcification 3) BAPE … A) Candle dripping and holly leaf sign B) Earliest, unilateral, hemorrhagic, exudative C) Crow feet sign
questions.exp: The pleura table reads 'Pleural plaques (X-ray : Candle dripping, Holly leaf sign)', 'BAPE ... Earliest, unilateral, hemorrhagic, exudative' and 'Visceral pleural calcification (X-ray : Crow feet sign)'. Subpleural linear densities parallel to the plaque are also listed under the plaques. (Book p227)

questions.sec: Chronic Asbestosis: Fibre Types, Industries, Pleural Plaques (Candle Dripping, Holly Leaf), BAPE Fluid Criteria, Crow Feet Sign, Shaggy Heart Sign and Parenchymal Fibrosis
questions.q: Which set of features is printed for BAPE (benign asbestos related pleural effusion)?
opts: The earliest finding; unilateral, hemorrhagic and exudative, with eosin >25% and mesothelial cells <50%
The latest finding; bilateral, serous and transudative, with eosin <50% and mesothelial cells <25%
The earliest finding; unilateral, hemorrhagic and exudative, with eosin <25% and mesothelial cells <50%
The earliest finding; bilateral, hemorrhagic and exudative, with eosin <25% and mesothelial cells <50%
questions.exp: The BAPE rows read 'Earliest, unilateral, hemorrhagic, exudative' and 'Eosin <25%, mesothelial cells <50%'. Both cell cut-offs are upper limits, and the fluid is exudative rather than transudative. (Book p227)

questions.sec: Chronic Asbestosis: Fibre Types, Industries, Pleural Plaques (Candle Dripping, Holly Leaf), BAPE Fluid Criteria, Crow Feet Sign, Shaggy Heart Sign and Parenchymal Fibrosis
questions.q: Bilateral lower lobe infiltrates with pleural plaques in asbestosis produce the ______ heart sign on page 227.
opts: Angel wing
Egg shell
Shaggy
Holly leaf
questions.exp: The parenchymal row reads 'Bilateral lower lobe infiltrates with pleural plaques : Shaggy heart sign' and 'Diffuse massive fibrosis (DMF) of lower lobe'. The shaggy heart border is produced by the adjacent pleural and parenchymal disease, not by cardiomegaly. (Book p227)

questions.sec: Chronic Asbestosis: Fibre Types, Industries, Pleural Plaques (Candle Dripping, Holly Leaf), BAPE Fluid Criteria, Crow Feet Sign, Shaggy Heart Sign and Parenchymal Fibrosis
questions.q: Which parenchymal clinical features of asbestosis are printed in the right-hand column?
opts: No clinical signs, with fibrosis detectable only on imaging and a normal PFT pattern
Chest pain, dyspnea, and fibrosis with bibasal coarse inspiratory crackle, no clubbing and an obstructive PFT pattern
Chest pain, haemoptysis, and fibrosis with apical fine crackles, clubbing and a restrictive PFT pattern
Chest pain, dyspnea, and fibrosis with bibasal fine inspiratory crackle, clubbing and a restrictive PFT pattern
questions.exp: The parenchyma column reads 'Chest pain', 'Dyspnea', and under 'Fibrosis': 'Bibasal fine inspiratory crackle', 'Clubbing' and 'PFT : Restrictive pattern'. The pleural column, in contrast, is the one printed with 'No clinical signs'. (Book p227)

questions.sec: Chronic Asbestosis: Fibre Types, Industries, Pleural Plaques (Candle Dripping, Holly Leaf), BAPE Fluid Criteria, Crow Feet Sign, Shaggy Heart Sign and Parenchymal Fibrosis
questions.q: TRUE or FALSE about pleural versus parenchymal asbestosis on page 227.
opts: False — both columns are printed as producing no clinical signs
True — the pleural column ends with 'no clinical signs', while the parenchymal column lists chest pain, dyspnoea and fibrosis signs
True — clubbing is printed under the pleural column only
False — the pleural column lists clubbing while the parenchymal column lists no signs
questions.exp: The pleura column's clinical cell reads 'Progressive dyspnoea, Chest pain, No clinical signs', whereas the parenchyma column lists chest pain, dyspnoea, bibasal fine crackles, clubbing and a restrictive PFT. Clubbing belongs to the parenchymal disease. (Book p227)

questions.sec: Chronic Asbestosis: Fibre Types, Industries, Pleural Plaques (Candle Dripping, Holly Leaf), BAPE Fluid Criteria, Crow Feet Sign, Shaggy Heart Sign and Parenchymal Fibrosis
questions.q: A shipyard worker has unilateral haemorrhagic pleural fluid with 20% eosinophils and 40% mesothelial cells. Which page 227 entity is this, and what is its temporal relationship to other asbestos findings?
opts: BAPE — the earliest asbestos-related pleural finding
BAPE — the latest asbestos-related pleural finding
Malignant mesothelioma — with a latency of 10–30 years
Pleural plaque with visceral calcification — the crow feet sign
questions.exp: BAPE is 'Earliest, unilateral, hemorrhagic, exudative' with 'Eosin <25%, mesothelial cells <50%'. The case values sit under both cut-offs, and BAPE is explicitly the earliest pleural manifestation, preceding plaques and calcification. (Book p227)

questions.sec: Asbestos Malignancy: Lung Cancer vs Mesothelioma Table, Ferruginous Body, Berylliosis as Delayed Hypersensitivity with Non-Caseating Granulomas and the Granuloma Differential
questions.q: Match each attribute with the asbestos-related tumour printed on page 228 — 1) Most common histology of lung cancer 2) Most common histology of mesothelioma 3) Latency of lung cancer 4) Latency of mesothelioma … A) > 30 years B) Adenocarcinoma > squamous cell carcinoma > small cell carcinoma C) 10–30 years D) Epitheloid > sarcomatoid
questions.exp: The table reads 'Adenocarcinoma > Squamous cell carcinoma > small cell carcinoma' for lung cancer and 'Epitheloid > Sarcomatoid' for mesothelioma, with latency '10–30 years' and '> 30 years' respectively. Mesothelioma has the longer latency. (Book p228)

questions.sec: Asbestos Malignancy: Lung Cancer vs Mesothelioma Table, Ferruginous Body, Berylliosis as Delayed Hypersensitivity with Non-Caseating Granulomas and the Granuloma Differential
questions.q: Which pair of smoking associations and clinical features is printed for lung cancer versus mesothelioma?
opts: Lung cancer: smoking association present, chest pain + mass; mesothelioma: smoking association absent, cough + haemoptysis
Lung cancer: smoking association absent, cough + haemoptysis; mesothelioma: smoking association present, chest pain + mass
Lung cancer: smoking association present, cough + haemoptysis; mesothelioma: smoking association absent, chest pain + mass
Lung cancer: smoking association present, cough + haemoptysis; mesothelioma: smoking association present, chest pain + mass
questions.exp: The row reads 'Smoking association — Present (lung cancer), Absent (mesothelioma)' and 'Clinical features — Cough + Hemoptysis versus Chest pain + mass'. Mesothelioma is the asbestos tumour not driven by smoking. (Book p228)

Within it, cat scratch disease is infective and Crohn's is inflammatory bowel disease; sarcoidosis is the idiopathic comparator for berylliosis. (Book p228)

units.title: Disease Types, Pneumoconiosis Definition, the Dust-Particle Size/Site Table, the Four Pneumoconioses and Byssinosis (Organic Dust, Monday Fever)
units.sec: Disease Types, Pneumoconiosis Definition, the Dust-Particle Size/Site Table, the Four Pneumoconioses and Byssinosis (Organic Dust, Monday Fever)
units.guide:
Occupational lung diseases (p223) divide into pneumoconiosis, occupational asthma and hypersensitivity pneumonitis. Pneumoconiosis is accumulation of dust in lung with tissue reactions to its presence.
Dust size decides the site: >3 µm lodges in secondary bronchi, 0.5–3 µm in the bronchiole and <0.5 µm in the alveoli, which is why the finest dusts cause parenchymal disease.
The four pneumoconioses are silicosis (most common), asbestosis, coal worker pneumoconiosis and berylliosis. Byssinosis is different — hypersensitivity to organic dust with recurrent Monday fever.

units.title: Silicosis: Industries, Crystalline vs Amorphous Silica, Parenchymal-Only Involvement, Malignancy/COPD Risk and the Acute-vs-Chronic Table (Exposure, Pathogenesis, Clinical Triangle, BAL, PFT, Prognosis)
units.sec: Silicosis: Industries, Crystalline vs Amorphous Silica, Parenchymal-Only Involvement, Malignancy/COPD Risk and the Acute-vs-Chronic Table (Exposure, Pathogenesis, Clinical Triangle, BAL, PFT, Prognosis)
units.guide:
Silicosis risk factors (p224) are mining, quarries, blast furnaces, slate industry, sand stone industry, ceramics and rock cutting. Crystalline silica (quartz) is most common, composed of SiO2 (free silica) and carries the higher occupational hazard; amorphous silica is the second type.
Features are lung parenchymal involvement with NO pleural involvement, plus a risk of malignancy and COPD.
Acute silicosis follows a large quantity over 2 years, has a dash for pathogenesis, presents acutely with severe dyspnea, hypoxia and weight loss, gives PAS-positive milky white BAL and has a very poor prognosis. Chronic silicosis follows 10–30 years, acts through injury to pulmonary alveolar macrophages with silicotuberculosis (reactivation of latent TB) and autoimmune illness (SLE, RA), gives chronic dry cough with dyspnea on exertion and chest signs in 25%, and shows a mixed PFT pattern.

units.title: Radiology of Silicosis: Acute Crazy-Pavement CT Pattern and the Chronic Nodule-to-PMF Sequence with Egg-Shell Calcification and Upper Lobe ILD
units.sec: Radiology of Silicosis: Acute Crazy-Pavement CT Pattern and the Chronic Nodule-to-PMF Sequence with Egg-Shell Calcification and Upper Lobe ILD
units.guide:
Acute silicosis CT (p225) shows the crazy pavement appearance: ground glass opacifications with intact lung structure, thickened septa and multiple centrilobular small nodules in the parenchyma.
Chronic silicosis progresses from small bilateral symmetric centrilobular parenchymal nodules to large conglomerate nodules with an angel wing appearance, ± cavitations, with hilar lymphadenopathy showing egg-shell calcification, then to progressive massive fibrosis, and finally upper lobe interstitial lung disease.

units.title: Crazy-Pavement Differential (DAH, AEP, PAP with Anti-GM-CSF), Coal Workers Pneumoconiosis, the CWP-vs-Silicosis Table and Caplan Syndrome
units.sec: Crazy-Pavement Differential (DAH, AEP, PAP with Anti-GM-CSF), Coal Workers Pneumoconiosis, the CWP-vs-Silicosis Table and Caplan Syndrome
units.guide:
The crazy pavement pattern (p226) also occurs in diffuse alveolar haemorrhage, acute eosinophilic pneumonia and pulmonary alveolar proteinosis — in PAP there are antibodies against GM-CSF causing abnormal clearance of surfactant, with PAS-positive milky white BAL.
CWP (black lung) shares with silicosis upper lobe involvement, injury to PAMs causing TB or autoimmune disease, ↑COPD, and parenchymal nodules >1 cm ± cavitations progressing to PMF; the pigment is carbon.
CWP versus silicosis: malignancy association present in silicosis and absent in CWP; hilar lymphadenopathy absent in silicosis and present in CWP; Caplan syndrome absent in silicosis and present in CWP. Caplan syndrome is CWP (necrobiotic nodule) plus rheumatoid arthritis with IgA rheumatoid factor positive plus active synovitis.

units.title: Chronic Asbestosis: Fibre Types, Industries, Pleural Plaques (Candle Dripping, Holly Leaf), BAPE Fluid Criteria, Crow Feet Sign, Shaggy Heart Sign and Parenchymal Fibrosis
units.sec: Chronic Asbestosis: Fibre Types, Industries, Pleural Plaques (Candle Dripping, Holly Leaf), BAPE Fluid Criteria, Crow Feet Sign, Shaggy Heart Sign and Parenchymal Fibrosis
units.guide:
Asbestos fibres (p227) are 90% serpentine/chrysotile with curly strands and less toxicity, and 10% amphibole with brittle long straight rods — crocidolite and amosite, amosite being more dangerous. Risk industries are textile, cement, ship building and automobile, and smoking adds parenchymal and malignant risk.
Pleura: parietal pleural calcification with pleural plaques (X-ray candle dripping, holly leaf sign) and subpleural linear densities parallel to the plaque; BAPE, the earliest finding, is unilateral, hemorrhagic and exudative with eosin <25% and mesothelial cells <50%; visceral pleural calcification gives the crow feet sign. Pleural disease is printed with 'no clinical signs'.
Parenchyma: bilateral lower lobe infiltrates with pleural plaques (shaggy heart sign) and diffuse massive fibrosis of the lower lobe, with chest pain, dyspnea, bibasal fine inspiratory crackles, clubbing and a restrictive PFT pattern.

units.title: Asbestos Malignancy: Lung Cancer vs Mesothelioma Table, Ferruginous Body, Berylliosis as Delayed Hypersensitivity with Non-Caseating Granulomas and the Granuloma Differential
units.sec: Asbestos Malignancy: Lung Cancer vs Mesothelioma Table, Ferruginous Body, Berylliosis as Delayed Hypersensitivity with Non-Caseating Granulomas and the Granuloma Differential
units.guide:
Asbestos malignancy (p228): lung cancer is adenocarcinoma > squamous cell carcinoma > small cell carcinoma with a 10–30 year latency, a present smoking association and cough with haemoptysis; mesothelioma is epitheloid > sarcomatoid with a > 30 year latency, no smoking association, chest pain with mass, and pathology markers pancytokeratin/calretinin with electron microscopy showing microvilli, desmosomes and tonofilaments. The lung cancer pathology cell is printed as a dash.
A ferruginous body is an asbestos body with a transparent core surrounded by iron and protein. Berylliosis is a delayed hypersensitivity with non-caseating granulomas, clinically similar to sarcoidosis; the non-caseating granuloma list is sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, lymphoma, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, cat scratch disease, berylliosis and Crohn's disease.

units.title: Berylliosis: Sarcoidosis Features That Are Absent, Industries, Upper Lobe ILD to PMF, Lymphocyte Proliferation Test, X-ray in 50% and the HRCT Triad
units.sec: Berylliosis: Sarcoidosis Features That Are Absent, Industries, Upper Lobe ILD to PMF, Lymphocyte Proliferation Test, X-ray in 50% and the HRCT Triad
units.guide:
Sarcoidosis findings absent in berylliosis (p229) are CNS symptoms, ocular symptoms, parotid findings and erythemoid lesions. Risk factors are ceramic industry, battery manufacturing and alloy industry.
Features are dyspnea with upper lobe ILD progressing to PMF. Investigations: lymphocyte proliferation test positive; chest X-ray normal in 50% of patients, with hilar adenopathy and ↑ interstitial markings in the remainder; HRCT shows the classical ground glass appearance with parenchymal nodules and septal lines.
